cells.tense: You are at the ledge and your pen is still moving across the page.
cells.ask: Begin the piece you keep circling — a first line, a rough build, a first call. Not ready. Just started, today.
cells.core:
You are at the ledge, and what comes next is not fully in view. That is where this works anyway: enough light for the next stretch, not the whole route. What makes it more than guesswork is where the imagining comes from. It is rising out of work you have already finished and taken in, not out of a wish. You are drawing on experience rather than skirting it.

So the invitation is to begin before the picture settles. You do not have to see how it ends. Take the making you have been turning over and make the plain first move — a draft, a sketch, a call — with no plan for the whole distance and no waiting for a clearer morning. If the step turns out wrong, that is information. Holding it another week is not.

cells.verb: walking with only the next stretch of ground lit
cells.place: the ledge where what is finished is set down and the next beginning starts

cells.tense: You will keep arranging a life around a thing that has not arrived yet.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: Handle the growing thing by what it actually asks for today, not by what the plan says is due. Ten honest minutes, nothing added.
cells.core:
You are out past the thing itself, making decisions from a picture of it. Schedules, promises, arrangements — all built around a version that has not shown up. From outside it looks like rooms furnished before the walls are poured. The imagery has stopped being a direction and become a place you are living in, and the real thing keeps getting compared to a rendering instead of being met.

Come back to the size it is. Handle it by what it asks for today rather than what the plan says is due. Then watch what that actually produces, in place of what you predicted. The picture sharpens by being corrected against something real, and you keep the aim. What you set down is only a timetable written for a stranger.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that is now behind you, still checking whether it was safe.
cells.act: sit with not knowing for ten minutes instead of filling it
cells.ask: Stay with a question you can't answer for ten minutes. No searching, no sorting, no closing it. When the time is up, stop.
cells.core:
You are past a door you are still arguing with. The habit here is to accept only what can be weighed and proved, and to treat everything else as noise — so the hunches, the sense of what something is before reasons arrive, get dismissed before they can land. You want the full map before the first step, and the price is too high, so you stay still.

A hunch arrives ahead of argument and does not need to win one. Sit with an unresolved question for ten minutes and refuse to fill it. What surfaces in that quiet is material, not decoration. It does not have to be trusted forever. Just stop overruling it before it has spoken, and see whether it turns out accurate.

cells.tense: A picture is steering what you make, and it has not signed its name.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Return to the plain exercise you keep meaning to pick back up — one sitting, alone, no additions and no upgrades.
cells.core:
There is a picture steering what you make, and you have not looked straight at it. You would say you are just working the way you work. But the same shape keeps turning up, and it has a source you have not named — the version of the finished thing you carry without noticing you carry it.

Bring it down to something plain and repeatable. Go back to the old exercise and run it the way it was the first time, with nothing added around it. Repetition without ornament is what shows you what you wanted before you wanted results. After several sittings the picture will be as legible as handwriting, and once you can read it, you can keep it or change it.

attempts.check: The record supports the mechanic (Feedback stage, Resonance channel, the four medicines and their acts), not any claim about what the person is dreaming, why, or what it cost them; so no cell locates a history or a motive. A reader could reasonably say the Too Much cell sounds like it is diagnosing daydreaming rather than vision that has outrun its processing, so that cell keeps to what is observable — planning built on a picture instead of on what happened. Each ask is one small act of the person's own medicine and stays usable even if the read is wrong, since it teaches them something about how they move regardless. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the balanced line about momentum being shared — it flatters a method, and it got cut.
